1.title: Two Départements, North and South
1.html:
The "région" of Alsace is made up of two "départements", conventionally distinguished by location:

🔵 Bas-Rhin (Lower Rhine, département 67) — north
Population about 915,000; capital Strasbourg; main towns include Haguenau, Molsheim, Saverne, Sélestat-Erstein and Wissembourg.
🟡 Haut-Rhin (Upper Rhine, département 68) — south
Population about 650,000; capital Colmar; main towns include Mulhouse, Altkirch, Guebwiller, Ribeauvillé and Thann.

💡 Memory tip: "Bas" (lower) is in the north and "Haut" (upper) is in the south because the names refer to the relative position along the Rhine (upstream/downstream), not to altitude on the map — beginners often mix them up, so take care.
2.title: Borders and Landforms
2.html:
• East and north: bounded by the Rhine (Rhin) and the Lauter, next to Germany — the Palatinate (Pfalz) to the north and, across the Rhine, Baden-Württemberg to the east
  • South: borders Franche-Comté
  • West: borders Lorraine
  • Vineyard distribution: a long narrow band along the eastern and southern foothills of the Vosges massif (Massif Vosgien) and the edge of the Rhine alluvial plain, at about 200–400 m, running roughly northeast–southwest
3.title: Two Key Rivers
3.items.0.label: Le Rhin (the Rhine)
3.items.0.desc: About 1,230 km long, rising in the Swiss Alps and flowing into the North Sea; forms Alsace's natural eastern border
3.items.1.label: L'Ill
3.items.1.desc: The Rhine's most important tributary, 208 km long, rising in the Alsatian Jura and passing Altkirch, Mulhouse, Sélestat and Strasbourg — the name "Alsace" (Elsass) is said to derive from an old phrase meaning "land along the Ill"
4.title: A Narrow Vineyard Strip and an Isolated Enclave
4.html:
Alsace's vineyards form a long north–south strip, from Thann in the south to Marlenheim and Nordheim in the north, about 100 km in total.

In addition, at the far north of Bas-Rhin next to the German border near Wissembourg, there is an isolated enclave about 2 km wide — the Cléebourg area, roughly 90 km from the main vineyard strip and the most unusual corner of Alsace geographically (covered in depth in Level 2).
5.question: The most commonly cited origin of the place name "Alsace" is linked to which of the following?
5.options.0: The name of an ancient Celtic tribe
5.options.1: The Ill river — the old phrase means "land along the Ill"
5.options.2: A rendering of the German pronunciation of the Rhine
5.options.3: The surname of a medieval lord
5.explanation: Alsace derives from the old form Elsass: El- comes from the Alemannic word Ell, referring to the Ill river that runs through Alsace from south to north and joins the Rhine; -sass comes from an old verb meaning "to sit, to be located". Together, Elsass literally means "land along the Ill" (Pays de l'Ill). This is the commonly cited theory; another leading theory holds that Alsace comes from Old High German Ali-saz / Elisaz, meaning "foreign land".
6.keyPoints.0: Alsace consists of two départements: Bas-Rhin (north, capital Strasbourg) and Haut-Rhin (south, capital Colmar)
6.keyPoints.1: "Bas" is in the north and "Haut" in the south — a reference to relative position along the Rhine, not altitude
6.keyPoints.2: Germany lies to the east and north (across the Rhine and the Lauter), Franche-Comté to the south and Lorraine to the west
6.keyPoints.3: Origin of the name Alsace: one common theory says the Ill river (the Rhine's most important tributary); another says Old High German for "foreign land"
6.keyPoints.4: The vineyards form a long north–south strip (Thann to Marlenheim, about 100 km), plus the isolated Cléebourg enclave
